weekLabel: Week 5 · Meeting A · Grouping, Outliers, and Defensible Summaries

slides.title: Turn many rows into one defensible comparison
slides.subtitle: Split-apply-combine, one function passed to .agg(), dual-rule outlier audits, and a key-based merge
slides.teaching: Open with: if you had 24 rows of room data, how would you compare North to South without inspecting every row by eye? Preview that groupby() answers this today, and that a single summary number still needs an outlier check before anyone should trust it.

slides.title: A summary is only as trustworthy as the grouping and the outlier check behind it
slides.statement: groupby() answers ‘compared to what’ — but a mean can hide one extreme value, and no single outlier rule catches everything.
slides.supporting: Today: split-apply-combine as the grammar behind every group comparison; functions passed in as arguments so each group can be summarized your way; and two named rules — IQR and z-score — for deciding which values deserve a closer look, including what to do when they disagree.
slides.teaching: Set up the whole session in one line: grouping tells a comparison story, outlier rules protect that story from being distorted by one bad or genuinely extreme row.

outcomes.head: Group
outcomes.body: Use groupby() to split a DataFrame into categories, apply summaries, and combine results.

outcomes.head: Rank
outcomes.body: Produce multiple aggregations in one call and sort the evidence table.

outcomes.head: Reuse
outcomes.body: Pass one function you wrote into .agg() or .apply(), then attach a grouped result with a key-based merge.

outcomes.head: Judge outliers
outcomes.body: Compare IQR and z-score flags, then decide keep / investigate / exclude in writing.

slides.teaching: Flag outcome 3 explicitly: Week 4 passed values as arguments; today a familiar function itself becomes the argument, written without parentheses.

items: Split, apply, combine: the grammar of groupby()
IQR vs. z-score decisions, then one key-based merge
slides.teaching: Tell students the whole session builds toward one dataset-level claim about Radley Hall that survives an outlier audit. Optional pandas convenience methods remain in the handout reference.

slides.title: Recall: Radley Hall, the shared teaching dataset

left.head: What it is
left.body: 24 rooms in a fictional building we're calling Radley Hall (not a real Slocum Hall record) — first opened in Week 4. Each row is one room: floor, zone (North/South), room_type, area_m2, energy_kwh_m2_yr, and a few more columns.

right.head: What Week 4 already found
right.body: One missing has_daylight value (room R303) and one missing energy_kwh_m2_yr value (room R206) — real reasons the Week 4 trustworthiness interview mattered. Today we group and compare; we are not re-cleaning.

slides.teaching: Keep this brief — a 60-90 second recall, not a re-teach. Confirm students still have last week's cleaned building_rooms.csv open or accessible.

slides.title: Split, apply, combine: the grammar behind every groupby()

steps.label: SPLIT
steps.head: Divide the rows
steps.body: Pandas divides the DataFrame into groups sharing one category value — every room where zone == 'South' becomes one group, every 'North' room another.

steps.label: APPLY
steps.head: Summarize each group
steps.body: The same function — mean, count, or a function you wrote — runs once per group, independently of every other group.

steps.label: COMBINE
steps.head: Rebuild one table
steps.body: Pandas reassembles one result per group into a single output table, indexed by the group labels.

slides.teaching: Draw this on the board as three literal piles of index cards if useful: split into a North pile and a South pile, summarize each pile, then rebuild one small table. This is the mental model for every groupby() call today.

slides.title: groupby(), defined

left.head: Definition
left.body: df.groupby(column) is a DataFrame method that divides rows into groups sharing the same value in column, so a later aggregation (like .mean()) runs separately per group instead of once over the whole table.

right.head: Example
right.body:
df.groupby("zone")["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].mean()

One mean is computed for every 'North' row, and a separate mean for every 'South' row — split-apply-combine, written in one line.

slides.teaching: Point out groupby() alone does nothing observable — it only becomes visible once an aggregation like .mean() is chained after it. Try printing df.groupby("zone") alone to show the unhelpful <DataFrameGroupBy object> repr.

slides.title: One line performs split, apply, and combine

parts.label: The DataFrame
parts.body: Radley Hall's 24 rooms, one per row.

parts.label: SPLIT
parts.body: Divides rows into a North group and a South group.

parts.label: Pick one column
parts.body: Selects a single column from each group — this is why the result is a Series, not a DataFrame.

parts.label: APPLY + COMBINE
parts.body: Averages each group's values, then rebuilds one result indexed by zone.

slides.teaching: Point at each numbered chip in turn: DataFrame, split, pick one column, apply-and-combine. Ask which chip would change if the call grouped by room_type instead of zone — only the SPLIT chip.

slides.title: Commit to an answer before you run the aggregation
slides.question: What does this print?
options: A DataFrame with columns zone and energy_kwh_m2_yr
A Series indexed by zone: North 64.25, South 115.68
The same Series, but South listed first because it has the higher mean
A SyntaxError, because .mean() and .round(2) cannot be split across lines
slides.why: A single-column selection returns a Series. Groups sort by zone name, not by mean — sort_values() ranks by value next.
slides.teaching: Poll hands for each option before revealing. Option C is the important trap: groupby() sorts by the group KEY, not by the result — sort_values() two slides ahead is the actual ranking tool.

slides.title: One line performs the whole split-apply-combine
slides.output:
zone
North     64.25
South    115.68
Name: energy_kwh_m2_yr, dtype: float64
slides.explainHead: Read the result as a Series
slides.explainBody: The output is a Series indexed by zone — recall Series from Week 4: one labeled column of values. South already looks much higher than North; the next slides make that comparison precise and complete.
slides.teaching: Run it live and ask: which zone uses more energy per square meter, and by roughly how much? Do not confirm the exact percentage yet — that is the headline table two slides ahead.

slides.title: Multiple aggregations in one call, using .agg()
slides.code:
zone_summary = df.groupby("zone").agg(
    mean_energy=("energy_kwh_m2_yr", "mean"),
    mean_area=("area_m2", "mean"),
    n=("room_id", "count"),
).round(2)
print(zone_summary)
slides.output:
mean_energy  mean_area   n
zone                             
North        64.25      40.98  12
South       115.68      38.25  12
slides.explainBody: Each keyword argument names a new column and states (source column, function) as a paired value in parentheses — Python calls this pairing a tuple, defined properly later this session. One .agg() call replaces three separate one-off summaries — and every result lands in one table, ready to compare.
slides.teaching: Point out mean_energy=, mean_area=, n= are keyword arguments naming the output columns — the same keyword-argument idea from Week 4's pd.read_csv(path, sep=','), now used to name results instead of configure a call.

slides.title: The headline finding: South rooms cost far more energy per m²
slides.callout: South-zone rooms use about 80% more energy per m² than North rooms — despite nearly identical average area and identical room counts. A plausible story: south-facing exposure driving cooling and solar loads. We will revisit this exact finding in Weeks 6 and 7.
slides.teaching: This is the finding to anchor for the rest of the Weeks 4-7 arc. Compute the percentage live: 115.68 / 64.25 = 1.80, so about 80% more — do not round this to 'double.' Ask what a designer would want to check before acting on it (sample size per zone, orientation mix, equipment load).

slides.title: sort_values() ranks a summary table
slides.output:
mean_energy  mean_area   n
zone                             
South       115.68      38.25  12
North        64.25      40.98  12
slides.explainHead: Sorting is a separate, explicit step
slides.explainBody: groupby().agg() does not guarantee any particular row order. sort_values(column, ascending=False) reorders the existing table — it does not recompute anything.
slides.teaching: With only two zones the reordering is subtle here; promise students the room_type table later in the session makes sort_values() far more useful, with seven categories to rank.

slides.title: A familiar function can be passed into .agg()

left.head: Recall Week 4, then extend it
left.body:
Week 4: you called a function with values, like pd.read_csv(path, sep=','). Today the function name itself can become an argument:

df.groupby("zone").agg(my_function)

right.head: What actually happens
right.body: agg() receives my_function without parentheses, then calls my_function(values) once for each group during split-apply-combine. You do not write the repetition yourself.

slides.teaching: Read the contrast aloud: my_function names the reusable procedure; my_function() would call it immediately. The next two code slides apply this to .agg(), then contrast it with .apply(), which receives the whole group instead of one column.

slides.title: .agg() accepts a function you defined yourself
slides.output:
zone
North     76.0
South    337.0
Name: energy_kwh_m2_yr, dtype: float64
slides.explainBody: energy_spread is an ordinary function from Week 3: def, a parameter, a return. .agg(energy_spread) — note: no parentheses after the name — runs it once per zone's values and combines the results, same split-apply-combine as 'mean'.
slides.teaching: Ask why South's spread (337.0) is so much larger than North's (76.0) — a preview that South also contains the extreme outlier room the class audits later this session.

slides.title: .apply() hands a function the WHOLE group at once
slides.explainHead: agg vs. apply: what the function receives
slides.explainBody: agg(energy_spread) passed one column's values. apply(zone_energy_spread) passes the whole group's DataFrame, so the function itself must select the column it needs — useful when a summary needs more than one column at once.
slides.teaching: Keep this brief: the two results match by design (same math), so the point is the difference in what arrives inside the function, not a new number to memorize.

slides.title: describe() summarizes a whole column at a glance
slides.callout:
df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"]
    .describe()

One call returns count, mean, spread (std), and the four quartiles. count is 23, not 24 — recall room R206's missing value from Week 4; describe() silently skips it.
slides.teaching: Point at max (410.0) sitting far above the 75th percentile (90.8) — that gap is exactly what the outlier rules ahead will formalize instead of eyeballing.

slides.title: value_counts() counts how often each category appears
slides.output:
zone
North    12
South    12
Name: count, dtype: int64
slides.explainHead: A quick sanity check before grouping
slides.explainBody: value_counts() answers 'how many rows in each category' — confirming a balanced 12-and-12 split here is exactly why the headline finding's comparison is fair: neither zone is being averaged from a much smaller sample.
slides.teaching: Ask what students would worry about if the split had been 20 North rooms and 4 South rooms instead — the same 80% gap would deserve far less confidence.

slides.title: room_type ranks program areas from largest to smallest
slides.callout:
df.groupby("room_type").agg(
    mean_area=("area_m2",
               "mean"),
    n=("room_id","count"),
)

Then .sort_values("mean_area") ranks the table. n matters as much as the mean: Gallery's 82.1 m² average rests on only 2 rooms.
slides.teaching: This table foreshadows the area_m2 outlier disagreement later this session — note how wide the room_type range already looks (3.0 to 82.1 m²) before any outlier rule is even applied.

slides.title: A group mean can hide one room that does not belong
slides.statement: Grouping compares averages. It says nothing about whether any single row is a measurement error, a genuine extreme, or evidence of a missing variable.
slides.supporting: Two named rules give that judgment a repeatable procedure: the IQR rule and the z-score rule. Applied to the same data, they usually agree — and today's second example shows exactly what it looks like when they do not.
slides.teaching: Transition slide — keep it short. The room to keep in mind here is R306 (Radley Hall's server closet), already visible as the max in the describe() table.

slides.title: IQR, defined
slides.definition: IQR — the interquartile range — measures the spread of the MIDDLE 50% of a sorted column: IQR = Q3 − Q1. One extreme value barely moves it, unlike a standard deviation, which every value affects.

example.head: energy_kwh_m2_yr: Q1 = 61.75, Q3 = 90.75
example.body: IQR = 90.75 − 61.75 = 29.0 kWh/m²/yr. The middle half of the 23 recorded rooms' energy values spans just 29 — small next to the 410.0 maximum.

slides.note: IQR alone is just a number — it doesn't flag anything. The IQR RULE, built from it on the next slide, adds the ×1.5 fences that actually flag a row.
slides.teaching: Point out IQR is exactly the 'box' in a box-and-whisker plot: Q1 and Q3 are the box's edges, IQR is its height. This slide names the number; the next slide builds an outlier rule from it.

slides.title: The IQR rule turns quartiles into an investigation boundary

steps.label: Q1
steps.head: Lower quartile
steps.body: Twenty-five percent of the values lie at or below Q1.

steps.label: Q3
steps.head: Upper quartile
steps.body: Seventy-five percent lie at or below Q3.

steps.label: IQR
steps.head: Middle spread
steps.body: IQR = Q3 − Q1 describes the middle half of the evidence.

steps.label: FENCES
steps.head: Flag, do not delete
steps.body: Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR identify rows to investigate.

slides.teaching: Write the two fence equations after tracing the visual sequence. Stress that 1.5 is a convention and a flag is not a verdict.

slides.title: .loc[] / .iloc[] and tuple-unpacking, defined

left.head: .loc[row, col]
left.body: Week 4 filtered rows with one condition and no column choice: rooms[rooms['zone']=='South']. df.loc[row_selector, column_selector] does both at once — row_selector picks matching rows (e.g. df["room_id"] == "R306"), column_selector names which column to keep. .iloc[0] then pulls the first value out of that filtered result BY POSITION — needed because the filtered Series keeps its original row label, not a fresh 0.

right.head: Tuple-unpacking
right.body: low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr computes two numbers on the right as one paired value — a tuple — then unpacks them into two names at once, in order, on the left. Every function that returns more than one value uses this same pattern.

slides.teaching: Write df.loc[condition, column] on the board next to Week 4's df[condition] — the second, comma-separated part is the only new part. Then write low, high = 1, 2 on the board and ask what each name holds before running any real code.

slides.title: Apply the IQR rule to energy_kwh_m2_yr
slides.code:
q1 = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].quantile(0.25)
q3 = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(low, high)

r306 = df.loc[df["room_id"] == "R306", "energy_kwh_m2_yr"]
print(r306.iloc[0] > high)
slides.explainHead: R306: a server closet at 410.0 kWh/m²/yr
slides.explainBody: low, high unpack the tuple from the line above; df.loc[row, col] then selects R306's row and its energy column, and .iloc[0] pulls that one value out by position (just defined). 410.0 is far above the high bound of 134.25, so the IQR rule flags room R306 — a server room running equipment around the clock is a real, physically plausible reason for extreme energy use, not obviously a data-entry error.
slides.teaching: Ask students to guess the room type before revealing it. 'Server' should feel like a satisfying, defensible explanation once shown — contrast this with the harder cases coming up on area_m2.

slides.title: z-score, defined
slides.definition: A z-score restates one value as 'how many standard deviations from the mean': z = (x − mean) / std. z = 0 means exactly average; z = 2 means two standard deviations above it.

example.head: The z-score rule
example.body: Flags any row where |z| > 2 (some fields use 3; this course uses 2) — a threshold the analyst states, exactly like IQR's ×1.5.

slides.note: One extreme value inflates the column's own std, which can shrink its own z-score. R306's std-inclusive z is 4.43; excluding R306 from both the mean and the std (leave-one-out) gives 17.26.
slides.teaching: Contrast the two rules conceptually before running code: IQR is based on quartiles (resistant to extremes); z-score is based on mean/std (sensitive to them) — exactly why they can disagree. The next code slide applies this rule to the same R306 example the IQR rule just caught.

slides.title: Wrap the IQR rule into two small documented functions
slides.explainHead: One function per pipeline stage, again
slides.explainBody: iqr_bounds and flag_iqr follow Week 4's convention - a docstring, type hints on parameters and return values - now applied to Week 5's rule. flag_iqr returns a Series of True/False, one per room: the same Boolean-Series idea from Week 2's comparisons, now produced by a function instead of one inline expression.
slides.teaching: Point out that flag_iqr calls iqr_bounds inside itself - one function calling another, a first preview of composing small functions instead of writing one long one.

slides.title: ...continued: apply it to every room, not just one
slides.output:
room_id   zone room_type  energy_kwh_m2_yr
17    R306  South    Server             410.0
19    R110  North    Closet              12.0
slides.explainHead: A low outlier the single-row check never found
slides.explainBody: The earlier slide only ever asked about R306. Running flag_iqr across the WHOLE column surfaces a second flagged room: R110, a Closet at only 12.0 kWh/m2/yr - below the rule's low bound, not above its high bound. A one-room spot-check would never have found it; applying the function to every room does.
slides.teaching: Ask what a suspiciously LOW energy reading might mean for a closet - a broken meter, an unused space, or a genuinely minimal-conditioning room - and contrast it with R306's high-side, equipment-driven story.

slides.title: The same two rooms, seen instead of listed
slides.alt: Strip plot of all 23 rooms' energy intensity with IQR band and 1.5-IQR fences; R110 at 12 and R306 at 410 fall outside the fences.
slides.caption: Every cleaned room plotted on one axis. Shaded band = the interquartile range; dashed lines = the 1.5-IQR fences the code just computed.
slides.explainHead: The rule is a picture before it is a formula
slides.explainBody: The printed table said R306 and R110 were flagged. This says why: the middle half of the building sits in a narrow band around 62-91, and R306's 410 is nowhere near it. R110's 12 is flagged for the opposite reason - a closet using almost nothing. Same numbers, same code, but the distance is now something you can point at.
slides.teaching: Ask which of the two flagged rooms looks more surprising. Most students say R306 because it is dramatic; R110 is the more interesting one, because a suspiciously LOW reading can mean a broken meter rather than an efficient room.

slides.title: Apply the z-score rule to the same column
slides.code:
mean = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].mean()
std = df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"].std()

r306 = df.loc[df["room_id"] == "R306", "energy_kwh_m2_yr"].iloc[0]
z = (r306 - mean) / std
print(round(z, 2))
print(abs(z) > 2)
slides.explainHead: Both rules agree: R306 is genuinely extreme
slides.explainBody: A z-score of 4.43 is far past the |z| > 2 threshold. On energy_kwh_m2_yr, the IQR rule and the z-score rule reach the same verdict — the clean case where two independent methods reinforce each other.
slides.teaching: State plainly: this agreement is the easy case. The next table shows the two rules pulling in different directions on a different column of the exact same dataset.

slides.title: IQR vs. z-score: two different lenses on one column

left.head: IQR rule
left.body: Built from quartiles (Q1, Q3) — the middle 50% of the data. Resistant to extremes: one huge value barely shifts Q1 or Q3. Flags a row outside Q1 − 1.5×IQR to Q3 + 1.5×IQR.

right.head: z-score rule
right.body: Built from the mean and std — every value pulls on both. Sensitive to extremes: one huge value inflates std and can even mask itself. Flags a row where |z| > 2.

slides.teaching: Say plainly: on energy_kwh_m2_yr the two rules just agreed (R306). The next table shows a real column, area_m2, where they do not — that disagreement is the point, not a bug in either rule.

slides.title: On area_m2, two rules disagree
slides.callout: IQR bounds are wide (−47.25 to 123.95) because this building mixes small offices and large studios. The 120 m² gallery fits inside that range but its z-score is 2.82. The 3 m² closet is flagged by neither rule.
slides.teaching: Ask whether the gallery is a valid program type or a suspicious record, and whether a 3 m² 'room' is legitimate. Numeric flags begin an investigation; they do not resolve context.

slides.title: The harder question underneath any flag

steps.label: MEASUREMENT ERROR
steps.head: Was it recorded wrong?
steps.body: A misplaced decimal, a unit mix-up, a sensor fault. Check the source before anything else — this is the only category where 'fix the number' is the right response.

steps.label: GENUINE EXTREME
steps.head: Is it really that different?
steps.body: R306's server load is a real, physically explainable extreme. Keep it in the analysis and say why.

steps.label: MISSING VARIABLE
steps.head: Is a category missing from the model?
steps.body: R110 (a closet on a room schedule) and R309 (a double-height gallery) both suggest the grouping itself — room_type, ceiling height — may need refining, not the row deleted.

slides.teaching: Emphasize: an outlier rule only produces a flag. Which of these three explanations applies is a judgment call the analyst has to defend in writing — exactly the keep/investigate/exclude sentence Meeting B will require for every flagged row.

slides.title: rename() and merge() combine small tables

left.head: rename(columns=...)
left.body: df.rename(columns={"zone": "zone_name"}) returns a copy with one or more column names changed — useful right before a merge, so the shared key column has a clear, matching name on both sides.

right.head: merge(other, on=...)
right.body: df.merge(other_df, on="zone", how="left") joins two tables on a shared key column, attaching other_df's columns onto every matching row of df — like a spreadsheet VLOOKUP, but explicit about which rows matched.

slides.teaching: Keep this brief and concrete — the next slide is the payoff: merging the zone summary back onto every individual room.

slides.title: Merge the zone summary back onto every room
slides.code:
zone_lookup = zone_summary.reset_index()[
    ["zone", "mean_energy"]
].rename(columns={"mean_energy": "zone_mean_energy"})
merged = df.merge(zone_lookup, on="zone", how="left")
merged["vs_zone_mean"] = (merged["energy_kwh_m2_yr"] / merged["zone_mean_energy"]).round(2)
cols = ["room_id", "zone", "energy_kwh_m2_yr",
        "zone_mean_energy", "vs_zone_mean"]
rows = merged["room_id"].isin(["R101", "R104", "R306"])
print(merged.loc[rows, cols].to_string(index=False))
slides.output:
room_id  zone  energy_kwh_m2_yr  zone_mean_energy  vs_zone_mean
   R101 North              62.0             64.25          0.96
   R104 South              95.0            115.68          0.82
   R306 South             410.0            115.68          3.54
slides.explainHead: Every room now knows its own zone's average
slides.explainBody: .isin([...]) keeps only the rows whose value matches an item in that list — here, three specific rooms for a compact printout — and .to_string(index=False) prints the DataFrame without pandas' default row-index column, purely for a cleaner readout. R306's own zone average is 115.68, and its own value is still 3.54× that average — confirming the outlier is extreme even against its own zone's already-higher baseline, not just the whole-building average.
slides.teaching: This exact merge — a group summary attached back onto per-row data — is the pattern Project 1 Part II requires; tell students explicitly that this slide is a preview of that milestone step.

slides.title: In-class check: rank room types by energy, not area
slides.prompt: Reuse the room_type table's pattern, but rank by mean energy_kwh_m2_yr instead of mean area_m2.
steps: Sort the result from highest to lowest.
Name the two room types nearest the top.
State one plausible reason — not a certainty — for the ranking.
slides.teaching: This reuses the room_type/area_m2 grouping pattern from earlier in the session on a different column, reinforcing that groupby().mean().round() is a general recipe, not a one-off. Ask students whether the energy ranking matches the area ranking from the earlier table — it should not match exactly, which is itself worth discussing.

slides.title: Audit an AI-generated outlier function
slides.prompt: AI wrote a z-score flag function that only checks one direction and treats every flag as a verdict.
steps: Explain why z > 2 (not abs(z) > 2) misses low outliers entirely.
Name the missing cross-check this function never runs.
Rewrite the return line to label a flag 'investigate', not delete it.
Confirm the repaired function still catches room R306.
slides.teaching: Show the AI code: def flag_outliers(s): return s[( (s - s.mean())/s.std() ) > 2]. The repair should use .abs() and should NOT silently drop flagged rows — tie this back to the three-category harder question from two slides ago.

slides.title: A comparison is only as strong as its weakest row
takeaways: groupby() is split, apply, combine — one line, three steps.
A function name can be passed into .agg() without calling it first.
IQR and z-score can disagree; that disagreement is evidence to interpret.
A key-based merge attaches group context back to each row.
slides.teaching: Exit prompt: ask students to name which room was flagged by both rules and which room was flagged by only one, then state the decision each flag requires.
